query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of tungsten (≈0.5 at.%) to the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix will yield a dual benefit by stiffening the alloy at low temperatures and promoting the in situ formation of a protective W‐enriched oxide—or glaze—layer at high temperatures, thereby maintaining a low coefficient of friction and low wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.intervention: Introduce a trace alloying addition of tungsten (around 0.5 atomic percent) during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Ball-on-disk sliding tests conducted in ambient air under controlled loads (e.g., ~20 N) and sliding speeds, with test temperatures spanning from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Tungsten atoms will cause lattice distortion and, at elevated temperatures, facilitate the heterogeneous nucleation of a continuous W‐enriched oxide or glaze layer at the wear interface.
generation.mechanism: At lower temperatures, tungsten-induced lattice distortion enhances hardness and mitigates adhesive wear, while at higher temperatures tungsten promotes friction-induced oxidation that generates a dense, low-shear oxide (possibly containing tungsten oxides) layer. This protective glaze minimizes both oxidative and adhesive wear, ensuring consistent tribological performance across the entire temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the pure CoCrFeNi alloy, the tungsten-modified alloy will exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate both at room temperature and at 800 °C, with smoother wear tracks and evidence of a stable, protective glaze layer forming during high-temperature sliding.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected under sliding wear conditions at moderate to high loads conducted in ambient environments, with temperatures specifically controlled from room temperature (≈25 °C) to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extrapolates the high-temperature wear benefits observed in tungsten-alloyed AlCoCrFeNi systems (e.g., evidence from PMC8470387 and PMC11278666) to a pure CoCrFeNi matrix. The precise phase evolution and glaze-layer formation in the absence of additional elements (such as Al or Ti) remain uncertain, and further study is required to confirm that the tungsten addition uniquely enables continuous lubrication over the full temperature range.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one with pure CoCrFeNi and one with CoCrFeNi containing 0.5 at.% tungsten. Perform identical ball-on-disk sliding wear tests on both samples at a series of controlled temperatures (room temperature, 150 °C, 500 °C, and 800 °C) under the same normal load and sliding speed in ambient air.
measurements: Quantify the coefficient of friction and wear rate at each test temperature.
Conduct surface morphology analyses (using SEM and EDS) to detect the formation and continuity of any oxide or glaze layer.
Perform phase analysis (via XRD) before and after testing to confirm tungsten-induced phase changes and oxidation products.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-alloyed CoCrFeNi does not exhibit a significantly lower and more stable coefficient of friction and a reduced wear rate relative to the pure alloy across the full temperature range, or if no continuous protective W-enriched oxide layer is observed at high temperatures, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The addition of vanadium changed the microstructure of the alloy. The microstructure of the Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy is two phase, consisting of a mixture of fcc and bcc phases with slightly different chemical compositions, mainly with different proportions of aluminum and chromium. On the other hand, the modification of the alloy with the addition of vanadium resulted in homogenization of the structure. The addition of vanadium increased the hardness of the material by about 33%. The proposed modification also increased the wear resistance of the alloy—the wear value decreased by 73%. Notably, the wear mechanism has also changed. In the case of the unmodified Al0.7CoCrFeNi alloy, the wear was of mixed adhesive–abrasive nature with the formation of a secondary layer. On the other hand, the Al0.7CoCrFeNiV0.5 alloy was dominated by abrasive wear with the presence of oxide wear products lifted from the friction zone.

AbstractFriction and wear properties of hot working die steel at above 800 °C are of particular interest for high temperature applications. Here, novel AlCoCrFeNiWx high-entropy alloy (HEA) coatings have been fabricated on the surface of hot working die steel by laser cladding. The effects of the as-prepared AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings on the microstructure and high temperature friction and wear behavior of hot working die steel are investigated through scanning electron microscopy (SEM), electron probe microanalysis (EPMA), X-ray diffraction (XRD), and X-ray absorption fine structure (XAFS). Having benefited from the formation of W-rich intermetallic compounds after the addition of W elements, the high temperature wear resistance of the coatings is obviously improved, and friction coefficient shows a large fluctuation. The microstructural characteristics of the AlCoCrFeNiWx HEA coatings after the high temperature wear resistance test shows a highly favorable impact on microstructure stability and wear resistance, due to its the strong lattice distortion effect of W element on BCC solid solutions and the second phase strengthening of the W-rich intermetallic compounds.
